title: React Miscellany ①
body:
## 1. getDerivedStateFromProps **What it is**: a class-only **static lifecycle method** that decides whether the newest props should update state. ```javascript class MyComponent extends React.Component { static getDerivedStateFromProps(props, state) { if (props.value !== state.prevValue) { return { prevValue: props.value, displayValue: props.value * 2 }; } return null; // no update } } ``` **The things that matter**: - It is static, so there is no `this` and no `this.setState`. You update state by returning an object, or return `null` for no update. - **It runs on every render**, including renders caused by the component's own `setState` — unlike `componentWillReceiveProps`, which fired only when the parent re-rendered (and did fire then even if the props had not changed) and never on the component's own `setState`. - It replaces the unsafe `componentWillReceiveProps`, which concurrent mode could call unexpectedly more than once. **Where it is used**: when state has to be force-synced to a particular prop — a list component that something outside can reset, for example. **In practice**: rarely. ① Class components are already uncommon in new projects. ② Even at their peak, the React team said this API is seldom needed and wrote a post arguing against overusing it — most cases are better handled another way, such as forcing a remount with `key`. Know what it is, be ready for the interview question, and leave it there. --- ## 2. Concurrent mode **The common misunderstanding**: it is not multithreading, and nothing runs simultaneously. The JS engine is still single-threaded. **What it actually means**: the render phase (`beginWork` / `completeWork`) **can be paused, abandoned, or restarted at any time**, without the user ever seeing a half-finished frame. That is the opposite of the traditional synchronous mode, where once rendering starts it has to run to the end. **An intuitive example**: typing in a search box. - Without concurrent mode: if the render triggered by the first character is expensive, it **blocks** the page and the second keystroke is stuck behind it. - With concurrent mode: on the second keystroke React **throws away** the unfinished work for the first, handles the higher-priority input first, and the box stays smooth. **The APIs**: `useTransition` and `useDeferredValue`, which let you mark an update as non-urgent and interruptible. ```javascript const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition(); function handleChange(e) { setInputValue(e.target.value); // high priority, update now startTransition(() => { setSearchResults(computeResults(e.target.value)); // low priority, interruptible }); } ``` --- ## 3. "Jotai is fully concurrent-friendly" — a claim that needs qualifying **The PDF's phrasing is misleading.** The truth is a trade-off between two technical routes, not "Jotai is good and the others are not". **Background — tearing**: during concurrent rendering React may pause and hand control back to the browser. If a data source that lives *outside* React (a Redux store, a Zustand store, a global variable) happens to change during that pause, **different components in the same render read the source at different moments** and the screen shows information that contradicts itself. **React's official answer**: `useSyncExternalStore`, introduced in React 18. Redux (react-redux v8+) and Zustand both use it, and both **avoid tearing** — so "only Jotai does not tear" is simply not accurate. **The real comparison**: | | Redux/Zustand (via useSyncExternalStore) | Jotai (via useState/useReducer) | |---|---|---| | Can it tear? | Never | Briefly, and it self-heals | | Smoothness with `useTransition` | De-optimised; some concurrency is given up (Zustand plus `useTransition` cannot show the pending state) | Fully smooth; real concurrent rendering | **Conclusion**: not black and white. It is "zero tearing" versus "fully smooth concurrency", and Jotai chose the second. --- ## 4. Portals **What they solve**: they decouple a component's **logical position** (its parent-child relationship) from its **physical DOM position**. It stays a child logically — props, context, and event bubbling all behave normally — while its DOM can be rendered anywhere on the page. **Where it matters**: when an ancestor has `overflow: hidden` or a CSS property that creates a new stacking context, a child modal or tooltip gets clipped or cannot sit above the page. Portalling it to `` escapes those constraints. ```javascript function Modal({ children }) { return ReactDOM.createPortal(children, document.body); } ``` **How often you write one**: not very. But the modals, tooltips, and select dropdowns in the mainstream UI libraries (Ant Design, MUI) are built on portals internally; it is just wrapped away. **The part most people miss**: the DOM moves, but **event bubbling still follows the React component tree, not the physical DOM** — because it goes through React's own synthetic event system. --- ## 5. What `react.d.ts` is The TypeScript declaration file at `node_modules/@types/react/index.d.ts`. **The key fact**: React does **not** maintain its own TypeScript types. They come from `DefinitelyTyped`, a community repository (`types/react/index.d.ts`) — a separate package, a different team, its own release cadence. **What it is for**: when you hit a type error or are unsure how to type an API, this file is the authority — more reliable than any blog post. `Cmd`/`Ctrl`-click any React API name in VS Code jumps straight to it. **Watch out**: because they are maintained separately, `react` and `@types/react` versions can drift. If something runs fine but TypeScript complains, or the reverse, suspect a version mismatch. --- ## 6. FID has been replaced by INP (since March 2024) **Update**: on 12 March 2024 Google removed `FID` (First Input Delay) from Core Web Vitals and replaced it with `INP` (Interaction to Next Paint). **Why**: FID only measured the delay on the user's **first** interaction. INP measures responsiveness across **every interaction in the page's lifetime**, taking the worst. **How that relates to React's concurrency**: the reasoning in the PDF — that concurrent mode lets the main thread respond to input sooner — is correct, but: 1. It should say "improves INP", not FID. FID is retired, and INP's whole-session measurement matches concurrency's goals better. 2. "Brings it earlier" is the wrong phrasing. FID and INP are durations; the goal is a smaller number, not an earlier one. ## 7. Suspense and error boundaries — the same entry point Two seemingly unrelated features go through the same function in the source: `throwException()`. Whatever a component throws during the render phase is caught here, and React **only checks whether it is a thenable** (an object with `.then`): ```js // react-reconciler/src/ReactFiberThrow.js if (value !== null && typeof value === 'object') { if (typeof value.then === 'function') { // This is a wakeable. The component suspended. ... // Mark the nearest Suspense boundary to switch to rendering a fallback. const suspenseBoundary = getSuspenseHandler(); ``` - Throwing a **Promise** → treated as "this component is waiting for data": walk up to the nearest ``, render its `fallback`, and retry the subtree once the promise resolves - Throwing an **Error** → walk up to the nearest error boundary (a class component defining `getDerivedStateFromError` or `componentDidCatch`) and let it render a fallback UI ### Suspense: missing data is also a kind of pause `React.lazy` and Suspense-aware data libraries (React Query, RSC) all use this: mid-render a component finds the data absent and **throws a Promise**. That is not an exception, it is a signalling mechanism — "I cannot render yet; call me when this promise settles". Note this is a different kind of pause from time slicing: time slicing yields voluntarily because the CPU has been held too long, Suspense suspends involuntarily because data has not arrived. It can stop a render without a single slice occurring. ### Error boundaries: class components only Function components still have **no** equivalent hook — write a class yourself or use `react-error-boundary`. The condition in the source is explicit: ```js case ClassComponent: if ( (workInProgress.flags & DidCapture) === NoFlags && (typeof ctor.getDerivedStateFromError === 'function' || (instance !== null && typeof instance.componentDidCatch === 'function')) ) { workInProgress.flags |= ShouldCapture; // mark this boundary to capture ... } ``` The two methods divide the work: | Method | Phase | Purpose | |---|---|---| | `getDerivedStateFromError` | render | Return new state to render the fallback UI | | `componentDidCatch` | commit | Receives the error and component stack, for logging | A minimal implementation: ```jsx class ErrorBoundary extends React.Component { state = { hasError: false }; static getDerivedStateFromError() { return { hasError: true }; } componentDidCatch(error, info) { report(error, info.componentStack); } render() { return this.state.hasError ?

Something went wrong

: this.props.children; } } ``` **The four kinds of error it cannot catch** (a frequent interview question): errors in event handlers, errors in async code such as `setTimeout` or promises, server-side rendering, and errors thrown by the boundary component **itself**. The reason is the same in every case — an error boundary can only catch what is thrown while React is **actively calling your code** during rendering or a lifecycle method. Event handlers and timers are invoked by the browser directly, with no React on the stack. Those need `try/catch` or a global `window.onerror`.
